questions.question: Which of the following organisations is known as World Bank?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**IBRD**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **IBRD (International Bank for Reconstruction and Development)** is one of the primary institutions of the World Bank Group.
 
• It was established in **1944** during the Bretton Woods Conference to provide financial and technical assistance for post-war reconstruction and development.
 
• IBRD provides loans and advisory services primarily to middle-income and creditworthy low-income countries, focusing on reducing poverty and promoting sustainable development.
 
• It offers long-term loans and guarantees at market-based interest rates to help countries finance large-scale projects such as infrastructure, healthcare, and education.
 
• The World Bank Group comprises five organizations, and IBRD acts as the initial and largest entity within the group.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **IMF (International Monetary Fund):**

 
 
• The IMF is an international financial institution established in 1944 to ensure global monetary cooperation, financial stability, and economic growth.
 
• It provides financial assistance to member countries facing balance-of-payments problems.
 
• The IMF primarily focuses on monetary policies, exchange rates, and economic surveillance, distinct from the World Bank's development-oriented approach.
 
• It offers short-term financial support and policy advice to help nations stabilize their economies.
 
 
 
• **ADB (Asian Development Bank):**
 
 
• The ADB is a regional development bank established in **1966** to promote social and economic development in Asia-Pacific countries.
 
• Its focus is on poverty alleviation, sustainable growth, and infrastructure development in member countries.
 
• Unlike the World Bank, which operates globally, ADB targets primarily regional development in Asia and the Pacific.
 
 
 
• **UNESCO (United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization):**
 
 
• UNESCO is a specialized agency of the United Nations established in **1945** to promote international collaboration in education, science, culture, and communication.
 
• It aims to build peace and foster sustainable development through knowledge-sharing and intercultural dialogue.
 
• UNESCO is not a financial institution but rather focuses on global educational and cultural initiatives.

questions.question: Economic planning is an essential feature of which of the following economies?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Socialist Economy**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• A socialist economy is characterized by **state ownership of resources** and centralized economic planning.
 
• Economic planning plays a crucial role in allocating resources and ensuring equitable distribution of wealth in a socialist economy.
 
• In this system, the government formulates **plans to guide production, distribution, and consumption** to meet the needs of society.
 
• The primary objective of economic planning in a socialist economy is to achieve **social welfare and reduce economic inequality**.
 
• Examples of countries that have adopted socialist principles in the past include the former Soviet Union and China during certain periods of their economic development.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Capitalist Economy**

 
 
• In a capitalist economy, resources are primarily owned by private individuals or corporations, and the market operates on the principles of supply and demand.
 
• Economic decisions are driven by profit motives rather than centralized planning.
 
• Examples of capitalist economies include the United States and most European countries.
 
• While economic planning may exist in some forms, it is not a defining feature of a capitalist system.
 
 
 
• **Dual Economy**
 
 
• A dual economy refers to an economic structure where two distinct sectors coexist: a modern industrial sector and a traditional agricultural sector.
 
• It is often observed in developing countries where industrialization is in progress.
 
• Economic planning may occur, but it is not the defining characteristic of this type of economy.
 
• Examples include many developing nations in Asia and Africa.
 
 
 
• **Mixed Economy**
 
 
• A mixed economy combines features of both capitalist and socialist systems, with both private and public ownership of resources.
 
• Economic planning exists but is not as dominant as in a socialist economy.
 
• In mixed economies, the government intervenes in areas where the market fails to ensure social welfare.
 
• Examples include India and France, where economic planning coexists with market-driven mechanisms.

questions.question: What is the official language of Indian state of Nagaland?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**English**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• English is the official language of the Indian state of Nagaland, as prescribed under Article 345 of the Constitution of India.
 
• It is used for all official purposes, including government communication, legal matters, and education.
 
• English acts as a unifying language in Nagaland, a state with significant linguistic diversity and multiple tribal languages.
 
• It also serves as a medium of instruction in schools and higher education institutions in Nagaland.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Naga**

 
 
• Naga is not a single language but rather a term referring to a group of languages spoken by the Naga tribes in Nagaland.
 
• There are more than 15 major Naga tribal languages, including Ao, Angami, Sumi, Lotha, and Konyak.
 
• Each tribe has its own distinct language and dialect, which are used primarily within the community for daily communication.
 
• Efforts have been made to preserve and promote these tribal languages, but they are not used as official languages.
 
 
 
• **Meitei**
 
 
• Meitei, also known as Manipuri, is the official language of the neighboring state of Manipur, not Nagaland.
 
• It belongs to the Sino-Tibetan language family and is spoken predominantly by the Meitei people of Manipur.
 
• Meitei is recognized as one of the 22 scheduled languages of India under the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution.
 
• It is used in government, education, and media in Manipur but has no official status in Nagaland.
 
 
 
• **Linguistic Diversity in Nagaland**
 
 
• Nagaland is home to over 16 major tribes, each with its own language and cultural identity.
 
• While tribal languages are widely spoken at the community level, English bridges the gap between different tribes and facilitates inter-tribal communication.

questions.question: How many spokes are there in the Ashoka Chakra depicted on the National Flag of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**24**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Ashoka Chakra depicted on the National Flag of India has **24 evenly spaced spokes**, symbolizing the 24 principles of life and righteousness.
 
• The Ashoka Chakra is inspired by the **wheel of dharma (dharma chakra)** from the Lion Capital of Ashoka, which is located in Sarnath, Uttar Pradesh.
 
• The 24 spokes of the Ashoka Chakra represent qualities such as love, courage, patience, peace, kindness, selflessness, and righteousness.
 
• It was adopted as a part of the Indian National Flag on **22nd July 1947**, shortly before India's independence on 15th August 1947.
 
• The Ashoka Chakra is blue in color and is placed at the center of the white band of the tricolor National Flag.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Ashoka Chakra**

 
 
• The Ashoka Chakra is a significant element of India's National Flag, symbolizing progress, dynamism, and the eternal wheel of law (dharma).
 
• The design is derived from the **Lion Capital of Ashoka, which is also the National Emblem of India.**
 
• The blue color of the chakra represents the vastness of the sky and the ocean, signifying continuity and eternity.
 
• The Ashoka Chakra emphasizes the importance of moving forward and adhering to ethical principles for the betterment of society.

questions.question: Where is the 'abolition of untouchability' articulated in the Constitution of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 17**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Article 17** of the Constitution of India explicitly abolishes the practice of untouchability and forbids its practice in any form.
 
• It states that "Untouchability" is abolished and its practice in any form is forbidden. The enforcement of any disability arising out of "Untouchability" shall be an offense punishable under the law.
 
• It is a fundamental right, categorized under Part III of the Constitution, ensuring equality and dignity for all citizens.
 
• The Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 (earlier known as the Untouchability Offenses Act, 1955) was enacted to prescribe penalties for the practice of untouchability.
 
• Article 17 reflects the ideals of social justice, equality, and human dignity, which are fundamental to the Indian Constitution.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 14**

 
 
• Article 14 guarantees "Equality before the law" and "Equal protection of the laws" within the territory of India.
 
• It ensures that all individuals are treated equally in the eyes of the law, prohibiting discrimination on grounds such as religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth.
 
• It forms the foundation for the principle of rule of law in India.
 
 
 
• **Article 15**
 
 
• Article 15 prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth.
 
• It also allows the state to make special provisions for women, children, and socially and educationally backward classes, including Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
 
• It plays a critical role in ensuring social justice and equality in India.
 
 
 
• **Article 16**
 
 
• Article 16 guarantees equality of opportunity in matters of public employment.
 
• It prohibits discrimination in employment or office under the state on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, or residence.
 
• The article aims to ensure fairness and merit-based recruitment in public services.

questions.question: During reign of Harsha, the Kannauj assembly was held to publicise the doctrines of which of the following sects?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mahayana**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• During the reign of Emperor Harsha, the Kannauj assembly (also known as the Kanauj Religious Assembly) was convened to promote the doctrines of the **Mahayana sect of Buddhism**.
 
• This assembly was attended by numerous scholars, monks, and dignitaries, including the famous Chinese traveler and Buddhist monk, **Xuanzang (Hiuen Tsang)**.
 
• Harsha himself was a patron of Mahayana Buddhism and actively worked to spread its teachings across his empire.
 
• The assembly served as a platform to discuss and publicize Mahayana Buddhist doctrines while emphasizing religious tolerance and harmony.
 
• Xuanzang, in his travel accounts, provided a detailed description of the assembly, highlighting its grandeur and Harsha’s dedication to the Mahayana sect.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Hinayana**:

 
 
• Hinayana, meaning the "Lesser Vehicle," is an early school of Buddhism that emphasizes individual salvation and self-discipline.
 
• It focuses on the original teachings of Buddha and the attainment of Nirvana through personal effort.
 
• The Theravada school, which is prominent in countries like Sri Lanka, Thailand, and Myanmar, is considered a part of Hinayana Buddhism.
 
 
 
• **Shwetamber**:
 
 
• Shwetamber (meaning "white-clad") is one of the two main sects of Jainism, the other being Digamber.
 
• Shwetamber monks and nuns wear white garments and emphasize the importance of scriptures in the Jain tradition.
 
• This sect focuses on non-violence (Ahimsa), truth, and asceticism as core principles.
 
 
 
• **Main Theme: Mahayana Buddhism**:
 
 
• Mahayana Buddhism, meaning the "Great Vehicle," emerged as a major school of Buddhism that emphasizes compassion and the liberation of all sentient beings.
 
• It introduced the concept of Bodhisattvas – enlightened beings who delay their own Nirvana to help others attain enlightenment.
 
• Key Mahayana texts include the Lotus Sutra, Heart Sutra, and the Diamond Sutra.
 
• Mahayana is widely practiced in countries like China, Japan, Korea, and Tibet.

• It was formed as a result of dissatisfaction with the **Non-Cooperation Movement**, which was withdrawn by Mahatma Gandhi in 1922 after the Chauri Chaura incident.
 
• The Swaraj Party aimed to contest elections to enter the legislative councils created by the Government of India Act, 1919, and oppose British policies from within.
 
• The party primarily sought to attain **self-governance (Swaraj)** within the British colonial framework through constitutional methods.
 
• C.R. Das served as the party's president, while Motilal Nehru became its secretary.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

questions.question: Where is the largest concentration of stupas in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Madhya Pradesh**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Sanchi, located in Madhya Pradesh, houses the largest concentration of stupas in India.** It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and renowned for its magnificent stupas and Buddhist art.
 
• The Great Stupa at Sanchi, commissioned by Emperor Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE, is one of the oldest stone structures in India.
 
• Sanchi has a total of eight stupas, along with other Buddhist monuments such as monasteries, temples, and pillars, which date from the 3rd century BCE to the 12th century CE.
 
• The site is an important center for the study of Buddhist architecture, as it represents early Buddhist art and is a key example of Mauryan architectural heritage.
 
• Stupas in Sanchi are significant for their intricate carvings, depicting events from the life of Buddha and Jataka tales.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Himachal Pradesh:**

 
 
• Himachal Pradesh is known for its Tibetan Buddhist monasteries, but it does not have a large concentration of stupas as compared to Madhya Pradesh.
 
• Key monasteries include Tabo Monastery, Key Monastery, and Dhankar Monastery, which are important spiritual and cultural sites for Buddhists.
 
• While stupas are present, they are generally located within monastery complexes and are fewer in number.
 
 
 
• **Bihar:**
 
 
• Bihar is the birthplace of Buddhism and home to several important Buddhist sites, such as Bodh Gaya, where Buddha attained enlightenment.
 
• Key structures include the Mahabodhi Temple and other stupas in Rajgir, Vaishali, and Nalanda.
 
• While Bihar has significant Buddhist sites, the concentration of stupas is not as dense as in Sanchi, Madhya Pradesh.
 
 
 
• **Uttar Pradesh:**
 
 
• Uttar Pradesh is an important region in the history of Buddhism, with sites like Sarnath (where Buddha delivered his first sermon) and Kushinagar (where he attained Mahaparinirvana).
 
• It has a few prominent stupas, such as the Dhamek Stupa in Sarnath, but the number and concentration are not as large as in Madhya Pradesh.
 
• The region holds immense historical and religious significance for Buddhists but lacks the architectural density of stupas found in Sanchi.
 
 
 
• **Stupas:**
 
 
• Stupas are dome-shaped structures that serve as Buddhist shrines, housing relics of the Buddha or other saints.
 
• They symbolize the path to enlightenment and are often surrounded by intricate carvings depicting Buddhist teachings and stories.
 
• The construction of stupas began during the time of Emperor Ashoka and spread across India and other parts of Asia.
 
• They are considered sacred spaces for meditation and worship in Buddhism.

questions.question: Thaipusam festival is celebrated by which of the following communities?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Tamil**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Thaipusam is a Hindu festival celebrated primarily by the Tamil community worldwide, including India, Malaysia, Singapore, Sri Lanka, and Mauritius.
 
• The festival is dedicated to Lord Murugan (also known as Kartikeya), who is regarded as the deity of war and victory.
 
• It is observed during the Tamil month of Thai (January-February) on the day of the full moon, which coincides with the Pushya star.
 
• Devotees often perform rituals such as carrying kavadis (ornate structures) or engaging in acts of penance to express gratitude or fulfill vows.
 
• The primary highlight of Thaipusam is the procession of devotees carrying offerings to the temple, often accompanied by music and chants.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Malayalam:**

 
 
• The Malayalam-speaking community primarily celebrates festivals such as Onam, Vishu, and Thrissur Pooram.
 
• Onam is the most prominent festival, marking the harvest season and the homecoming of King Mahabali.
 
• Vishu, another key festival, signifies the beginning of the Malayalam New Year.
 
 
 
• **Telugu:**
 
 
• The Telugu-speaking community celebrates festivals like Ugadi, Sankranti, and Dasara.
 
• Ugadi marks the Telugu New Year and is celebrated with traditional food, cultural activities, and prayers.
 
• Sankranti is a harvest festival, widely known for its kite-flying competitions and traditional feasts.
 
 
 
• **Marathi:**
 
 
• The Marathi-speaking community celebrates festivals such as Ganesh Chaturthi, Gudi Padwa, and Diwali.
 
• Ganesh Chaturthi, honoring Lord Ganesha, is the most significant festival for this community, characterized by elaborate pujas and processions.
 
• Gudi Padwa marks the Marathi New Year and is celebrated with cultural performances and traditional dishes.

questions.question: Which of the following states as the largest forest area?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Madhya Pradesh**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Madhya Pradesh** has the largest forest cover area in India according to the Forest Survey of India report.
 
• The total forest area of Madhya Pradesh is approximately **77,493 square kilometers**, constituting around 25.14% of the state's geographical area.
 
• The state is home to major national parks and wildlife sanctuaries such as Kanha, Bandhavgarh, and Satpura, contributing significantly to its forest cover.
 
• Madhya Pradesh's forests are rich in biodiversity, with a variety of flora and fauna, including teak, sal, bamboo, and endangered species such as Bengal tiger and Indian leopard.
 
• It plays a crucial role in India's ecological balance by acting as a carbon sink and providing livelihood opportunities to tribal and forest-dependent communities.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Bihar**

 
 
• Bihar has relatively low forest cover, accounting for only about **7.84****% of its geographical area**.
 
• The state’s forests are primarily deciduous and are concentrated in regions like Kaimur, Rohtas, and Gaya.
 
• Bihar's forest resources are limited, and the state focuses more on agriculture and urban development.
 
 
 
• **Karnataka**
 
 
• Karnataka has a significant forest cover of approximately **20.19% of its geographical area**, which amounts to around 37,550 square kilometers.
 
• The state is known for its Western Ghats, which are a biodiversity hotspot and home to dense evergreen forests.
 
• Karnataka's forests support various wildlife species, including elephants, tigers, and unique flora like sandalwood trees.
 
 
 
• **Kerala**
 
 
• Kerala's forest cover is around **27.79%**** of its geographical area**, making it one of the greenest states in India.
 
• The state's forests are primarily tropical moist deciduous and evergreen types, found in the Western Ghats.
 
• Kerala's biodiversity includes rare species such as the Nilgiri tahr and the Malabar civet.

questions.question: Ken River is the tributary of which of the following river?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Yamuna**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Ken River is a major tributary of the **Yamuna River**, which is one of the most important rivers in India.
 
• It originates from the **Kaimur Hills in Madhya Pradesh** and flows northward through the Bundelkhand region.
 
• The Ken River is renowned for its **scenic beauty** and flows through the **Panna Tiger Reserve**, known for its diverse wildlife.
 
• The confluence of the Ken and Yamuna Rivers is located near **Chilla village in Uttar Pradesh**.
 
• The Ken-Betwa River Interlinking Project is a significant development initiative aimed at transferring water from the Ken River to the Betwa River to address water scarcity in the Bundelkhand region.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Tapti River:**

 
 
• The Tapti River originates from the **Satpura ranges** in Madhya Pradesh and flows westward into the Arabian Sea.
 
• It is one of the major rivers of peninsular India, along with the Narmada and Mahi rivers, that flows westward.
 
• It passes through Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Gujarat before draining into the sea.​
 
 
 
• **Krishna**
 
 
• Originates at Mahabaleshwar (Maharashtra).
 
• Major tributaries: Ghatprabha, Malaprabha, Tungabhadra.
 
• Largest basin area in Karnataka.
 
 
 
• **Godavari**
 
 
• Longest peninsular river, called Dakshin Ganga.
 
• Rises in Trimbak (Nasik, Maharashtra).
 
• Major tributaries: Pravara, Manjira, Indravati, Sabari.
 
 
 
• **Yamuna River:**
 
 
• The Yamuna is the second-largest tributary river of the Ganges and originates from the **Yamunotri Glacier in Uttarakhand**.
 
• It flows through several states, including Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, Haryana, Delhi, and Uttar Pradesh.
 
• Major cities like Delhi, Mathura, and Agra are situated along its banks.
 
• The Yamuna is a lifeline for agricultural and industrial activities in northern India.

questions.question: Manipur has common boundaries with which of the group of state?

The correct answer is __**Nagaland, Mizoram and Assam**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Manipur** shares its boundaries with three Indian states: Nagaland to the north, Mizoram to the south, and Assam to the west.
 
• It also has an international border with Myanmar to the east.

questions.question: The Himalayan mountain range is an example of ________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Fold mountain**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Himalayan mountain range is classified as a **Fold Mountain**, formed as a result of the collision between the Indian Plate and the Eurasian Plate.
 
• Fold mountains are created through the process of **continental plate convergence**, leading to the folding and uplifting of sedimentary rock layers.
 
• The Himalayas are considered **young fold mountains** as they are geologically new, formed approximately 40-50 million years ago.
 
• This mountain range consists of **three parallel ranges**—the Greater Himalayas, Lesser Himalayas, and Shivalik Hills, exhibiting diverse geological features.
 
• Fold mountains, including the Himalayas, are characterized by **lofty peaks, steep slopes, deep valleys, and fertile basins**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Rock Mountain:**

 
 
• This term is not commonly used in geological classifications; it can broadly refer to mountains made of solid rock formations.
 
• Mountains predominantly made of igneous, sedimentary, or metamorphic rocks are examples, but the term lacks specificity in scientific contexts.
 
• The Himalayas are not classified as "rock mountains" as their formation is linked to tectonic activity and folding processes.
 
 
 
• **Block Mountain:**
 
 
• Block mountains are formed due to **faulting and fracturing** in the Earth's crust caused by tensional forces.
 
• These mountains are characterized by the uplift of large blocks of Earth's crust, while adjacent blocks sink to form rift valleys.
 
• Examples include the **Vosges Mountains in Europe** and the **Sierra Nevada in the USA**. The Himalayas are not block mountains as their origin is linked to folding rather than faulting.
 
 
 
• **Volcanic Mountain:**
 
 
• Volcanic mountains are formed due to the accumulation of lava, ash, and other volcanic materials emitted during volcanic eruptions.
 
• These mountains are typically conical in shape and include peaks such as **Mount Fuji in Japan** and **Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania**.
 
• The Himalayas are not volcanic mountains, as they were formed by tectonic plate collision rather than volcanic activity.
 
 
 
• **The Formation of Himalayan Mountains:**
 
 
• The Himalayas are the result of the ongoing collision between the Indian Plate and the Eurasian Plate.
 
• This collision caused the sedimentary rocks in the Tethys Ocean to fold and uplift, giving rise to the Himalayan range.
 
• The Himalayas continue to rise due to tectonic activity, making them one of the youngest and most dynamic mountain ranges in the world.

__
 
• **Humidity** is a key element of weather that refers to the amount of water vapor present in the air.
 
• It significantly affects weather conditions, including precipitation, fog formation, and the overall comfort level of the atmosphere.
 
• Humidity is measured in terms of absolute, relative, or specific humidity, with relative humidity being the most commonly used in weather forecasting.

• **Weather vs Climate:**
 
 
• Weather
 
 
• Refers to the short-term atmospheric conditions of a place.

• Climate

questions.question: What is the scale used for measuring the intensity of the earthquake?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Richter Scale**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Richter Scale was developed in 1935 by Charles F. Richter in collaboration with Beno Gutenberg at the California Institute of Technology.
 
• It is a logarithmic scale used to measure the intensity of seismic waves or the magnitude of earthquakes.
 
• Each whole number increase on the Richter Scale corresponds to a tenfold increase in measured amplitude and approximately 31.6 times more energy release.
 
• The scale ranges from 0 to 9+, with earthquakes below magnitude 2.0 often not felt, while those above magnitude 7 can cause significant damage.
 
• While widely used, the Richter Scale is most effective for measuring local earthquakes and has been largely replaced by the Moment Magnitude Scale for global applications.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Metric Scale**

 
 
• The Metric Scale is not related to earthquake measurement. It refers to the standard system of measurement based on meters, grams, and liters used in scientific and everyday applications globally.
 
• It is crucial for ensuring uniformity in measurements across various fields such as engineering, commerce, and daily life.
 
 
 
• **Epicentre Scale**
 
 
• The term "Epicentre" refers to the point on the Earth's surface directly above the earthquake's origin (focus).
 
• There is no "Epicentre Scale" for measuring earthquakes; instead, the epicentre is a geographical reference for locating the earthquake's impact area.
 
 
 
• **Quake Scale**
 
 
• The "Quake Scale" is not an established or recognized term in seismology.
 
• Earthquake magnitudes are measured using scales like the Richter Scale or Moment Magnitude Scale, while intensity is assessed using the Modified Mercalli Intensity (MMI) scale.
 
 
 
• **Additional Information on Earthquake Measurement**
 
 
• The Moment Magnitude Scale (Mw) is now preferred for measuring large earthquakes globally, as it is more accurate for assessing the total energy released.
 
• The Modified Mercalli Intensity (MMI) Scale measures the intensity of earthquakes based on observed effects on people, buildings, and the Earth's surface.

questions.question: Which one of the following has the highest value of specific heat?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Water**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Water** has the highest specific heat capacity among the given options, which is approximately **4.18 J/g°C**.
 
• This high specific heat capacity enables water to absorb and store a large amount of heat energy with minimal temperature change, making it a vital component in regulating temperature in natural and biological processes.
 
• The high specific heat is due to the strong hydrogen bonding between water molecules, which requires significant energy to break.
 
• Water’s ability to retain heat makes it an excellent coolant and plays a key role in maintaining environmental and biological homeostasis.
 
• Applications of water’s high specific heat include its use in thermal regulation, climate control, and its role as a heat reservoir in oceans and seas.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Alcohol**

 
 
• Alcohols, such as ethanol, have a specific heat capacity of approximately **2.44 J/g°C**, which is lower than water.
 
• Alcohols exhibit weaker intermolecular forces compared to water due to the absence of extensive hydrogen bonding, leading to a lower heat capacity.
 
• Alcohol’s lower specific heat makes it a poor thermal regulator but suitable as a solvent or fuel.
 
 
 
• **Methane**
 
 
• Methane (CH4) has a specific heat capacity of around **2.22 J/g°C**, which is much lower than water.
 
• As a non-polar molecule, methane lacks hydrogen bonding, resulting in lower energy requirements to increase its temperature.
 
• Methane is primarily used as a fuel source and is a major component of natural gas.
 
 
 
• **Kerosene**
 
 
• Kerosene, a hydrocarbon mixture, has a specific heat capacity of approximately **2.1 J/g°C**, which is also lower than water.
 
• Its low specific heat makes kerosene efficient as a fuel for heating and energy production but unsuitable for thermal regulation.
 
• Kerosene is widely used in aviation fuel, lighting, and heating applications.

questions.question: Which of the following quanuae nains constant when an artificial Satellite revolves around the Earth in circular orbit?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Angular Momentum**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• When an artificial satellite revolves around the Earth in a circular orbit, its **angular momentum remains constant** as no external torque acts on the system.
 
• **Angular momentum (L)** is given by the formula L = mvr, where m is the mass of the satellite, v is its velocity, and r is the radius of the circular orbit.
 
• In a circular orbit, both the radius (r) and the mass (m) of the satellite remain constant, and the velocity of the satellite adjusts to satisfy the equilibrium condition, ensuring constant angular momentum.
 
• This phenomenon is explained by the principle of conservation of angular momentum, which states that in the absence of an external torque, the angular momentum of a system remains conserved.
 
• Angular momentum conservation is a crucial concept in celestial mechanics and is responsible for the stable motion of satellites and planets in their orbits.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Linear Velocity:**

 
 
• Linear velocity (v) of the satellite is the speed at which it moves along the circular path, given by v = √(GM/r), where G is the gravitational constant, M is the mass of the Earth, and r is the radius of the orbit.
 
• It does not remain constant for orbits other than circular, as it depends on the orbital radius.
 
• In elliptical orbits, the linear velocity varies as the satellite moves closer to or farther from the central body due to changes in gravitational force.
 
 
 
• **Angular Displacement:**
 
 
• Angular displacement refers to the angle covered by the satellite in its orbit over a certain period of time.
 
• It is a measure of the change in the satellite's position relative to the center of the circular orbit.
 
• Angular displacement is not constant as it depends on the time interval being considered.

__
 
• **Presbyopia** is an age-related condition where the lens of the eye loses its elasticity, making it difficult to focus on close objects.
 
• **Bifocal lenses** are specially designed to correct presbyopia by providing two optical powers: one for distance vision (upper part) and another for near vision (lower part).
 
• Bifocal lenses help users focus on objects at varying distances without the need for multiple pairs of glasses.
 
• The design of bifocal lenses makes them a practical solution for individuals experiencing both near and far vision problems, commonly due to aging.
 
• Bifocal lenses are widely recommended for older adults, as presbyopia typically begins to affect individuals after the age of 40.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Concave lenses**

 
 
• Concave lenses are used to correct **myopia (nearsightedness)**, a condition where distant objects appear blurry.
 
• They diverge light rays before they reach the retina, helping focus the image correctly on the retina.
 
 
 
• **Convex lenses**
 
 
• Convex lenses are used to correct **hypermetropia (farsightedness)**, a condition where close objects appear blurry.
 
• They converge the light rays so that the focus falls directly on the retina.
 
 
 
• **Cylindrical lenses**
 
 
• Cylindrical lenses are used to correct **astigmatism**, a condition caused by an irregularly shaped cornea or lens.
 
• They focus light in one direction only, correcting the uneven focusing caused by astigmatism.
 
 
 
• **Progressive lenses**
 
 
• Progressive lenses are an advanced alternative to bifocals, offering a gradual transition in optical power for seamless vision at all distances.
 
• They eliminate the visible line present in bifocal lenses, providing a more natural and aesthetic experience for users.

questions.question: Which among the following blood protein regulates the amount of water in plasma?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Albumin**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Albumin** is the primary protein found in blood plasma and plays a crucial role in maintaining osmotic pressure, which regulates the balance of water between blood and surrounding tissues.
 
• It is synthesized by the liver and constitutes approximately 60% of the total plasma protein in humans.
 
• Albumin prevents the leakage of blood into interstitial spaces and ensures proper blood volume and pressure are maintained.
 
• It also acts as a carrier protein, transporting hormones, vitamins, drugs, and ions through the bloodstream.
 
• A deficiency in albumin can lead to edema (fluid retention) because the osmotic pressure needed to keep water in the blood vessels is reduced.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Globulin:**

 
 
• Globulins are a group of proteins in the blood plasma that include alpha, beta, and gamma globulins.
 
• They are involved in immune function and act as transporters for lipids, hormones, and other molecules.
 
• Gamma globulins specifically consist of antibodies that help the body fight infections.
 
• Globulins do not play a direct role in regulating water balance in plasma.
 
 
 
• **Fibulin:**
 
 
• Fibulin is not a blood protein involved in water regulation; rather, it is part of the extracellular matrix.
 
• It is associated with elastic fibers and contributes to tissue integrity and elasticity.
 
• Fibulin does not influence osmotic pressure or water balance in plasma.
 
 
 
• **Plasma and its Components:**
 
 
• Blood plasma is the liquid component of blood and comprises about 55% of total blood volume.
 
• It consists of water (about 90%), electrolytes, nutrients, hormones, waste products, and proteins such as albumin, globulin, and fibrinogen.
 
• The proteins in plasma have various roles, including maintaining osmotic pressure, immune defense, and clotting.
 
• Albumin is the most abundant protein in plasma, while globulins and fibrinogen serve other specialized functions.

 C + H₂O → CO + H₂.

questions.question: Isobar is produced by the emission of which of the following?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Beta ray**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Isobars are atoms of different chemical elements that have the same mass number but different atomic numbers.
 
• Beta decay results in the emission of a beta particle (electron or positron) from the nucleus of an atom.
 
• During beta decay, a neutron is converted into a proton (or vice versa), altering the atomic number but keeping the mass number constant, leading to the formation of isobars.
 
• The mass number remains unchanged in beta decay because the loss of a neutron and the gain of a proton do not affect the total nucleon count.
 
• Beta radiation is commonly observed in radioactive isotopes such as carbon-14 and potassium-40, which undergo decay processes that produce isobars.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Alpha ray:**
 
 
• Alpha rays consist of helium nuclei (2 protons and 2 neutrons) emitted during alpha decay.
 
• Alpha decay typically occurs in heavy nuclei, such as uranium-238 or radium-226.
 
• This process reduces the atomic number by 2 and the mass number by 4, resulting in the formation of a new element rather than isobars.
 
• Alpha particles have low penetration power and can be stopped by a sheet of paper or human skin.
 
 
 
• **Gamma ray:**
 
 
• Gamma rays are high-energy electromagnetic waves emitted during the transition of a nucleus from an excited state to a lower energy state.
 
• Unlike beta or alpha decay, gamma radiation does not alter the atomic number or mass number of an atom.
 
• Gamma rays have high penetration power and require dense materials like lead or concrete for shielding.
 
• They are often emitted alongside alpha or beta particles during radioactive decay processes.
 
 
 
• **X-ray:**
 
 
• X-rays are electromagnetic waves with wavelengths shorter than ultraviolet light but longer than gamma rays.
 
• They are produced when electrons transition between energy levels in an atom or when high-energy electrons strike a metal target.
 
• X-rays are widely used in medical imaging and diagnostic applications but do not play a role in the formation of isobars.
 
 
 
• **General Concept of Isobars:**
 
 
• Isobars are crucial in studying nuclear reactions and radioactive decay mechanisms.
 
• Examples of isobars include carbon-14 (6 protons, 8 neutrons) and nitrogen-14 (7 protons, 7 neutrons), both having a mass number of 14.
 
• The study of isobars helps scientists understand energy stability and decay processes in nuclei.

questions.question: Which of the following consists of the highest biodiversity?

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Tropical rainforests are the richest ecosystems on Earth** and host the highest biodiversity, with millions of species of plants, animals, fungi, and microorganisms.
 
• They cover approximately **6-7% of Earth's surface** but are home to more than half of the species globally.
 
• Tropical rainforests are characterized by **warm temperatures, high humidity, and consistent rainfall** throughout the year, creating ideal conditions for diverse flora and fauna.
 
• Regions like the Amazon Basin, Congo Basin, and Southeast Asia are examples of tropical rainforests, which support countless species including endangered ones.
 
• These forests play a critical role in regulating the global climate, maintaining oxygen levels, and storing carbon, making them essential for environmental stability.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Temperate Forest:**

 
 
• Temperate forests are found in regions with moderate climates, typically between tropical and polar zones.
 
• They exhibit **seasonal variations** with warm summers and cold winters, supporting species adapted to these changes.
 
• While temperate forests have a rich biodiversity, it is relatively lower compared to tropical rainforests.
 
• Common species include oak, maple, deer, wolves, and bears.
 
 
 
• **Deciduous Forest:**
 
 
• Deciduous forests are characterized by trees that shed their leaves annually during the autumn season.
 
• These forests are found in temperate regions and support a variety of species, such as squirrels, foxes, and migratory birds.
 
• Though diverse, their biodiversity is not as extensive as tropical rainforests.
 
• Examples include forests in parts of Europe, North America, and East Asia.
 
 
 
• **Grasslands:**
 
 
• Grasslands are ecosystems dominated by grasses and are found in regions with seasonal droughts and fires.
 
• They support species like bison, antelope, and prairie dogs, but have **lower biodiversity** compared to forests.
 
• Grasslands are divided into tropical (savannas) and temperate types, and they are key habitats for grazing herbivores.
 
• Examples include the prairies of North America and the savannas of Africa.

questions.question: Graphite is an allotrope of _______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Carbon**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Graphite**__ is an __**allotrope**__ of **__Carbon__**.

 __
 
• An **allotrope **is a chemical element that **exists in two or more different forms**, each with a **unique physical structure** but the **same chemical composition**.
 
• **Graphite **is a naturally occurring form of **crystalline carbon**.
 
• Its atoms are arranged in a **hexagonal** structure.
 
• It is **extremely soft, cleaves **with **very light pressure**, and has very** low specific gravity**.
 
• Under **high pressures and temperatures**, it converts to **diamond**.
 
• It is a native element mineral found in **metamorphic **and **igneous **rocks.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Properties of Graphite** :

 
 
• Graphite has carbon atoms arranged in sheets of the hexagon and has sp2 hybridization.
 
• Carbon uses only 3 electrons in bonding and hence 1 electron is spare.
 
• Graphite has a high melting point.
 
• Graphite is insoluble in water and organic solvents.
 
• This free electron of each carbon atom in graphite is responsible for the conduction of electricity.
